This is in line with our previous finding that blocking the ER-Golgi vesicular cycling abolished the formation of liquid viral inclusions [ 4 ]. Although it was proposed that the recycling endosome is the primary reservoir of ATG9A for autophagosome initiation [ 42 ], we found that the main pool of ATG9A mobilized during IAV infection originated from the Golgi/TGN (Figs 2C and 3A ) and that the effect of ATG9A was independent yet synergic with that of Rab11a in IAV infection. In fact, when overexpressed, ATG9A localizes between the ER and viral inclusions. This raises the hypothesis that when ATG9A is not functioning at the ER, vRNP-Rab11a endosomes circulate in microtubules but are unable to concentrate at ERES and, hence, do not form optimal viral inclusions. We think this effect is specific to IAV infection. Supporting the specificity of the observed effect is a recent study showing that IAV manipulates Rab11a endosome transport by reducing its association to dynein [ 16 ]. We cannot exclude, however, the possibility that ATG9A interacts with other regulators of the recycling endosome, such as Rab11b. In our study, we also addressed ATG9A significance and changes in liquid condensate shape to IAV production. We showed that, in the absence of ATG9A, there are less virions budding the cell, but released virions contain correct amounts of complete genomes ( Fig 7D and 7E ). This suggests that the cellular environment to create complete genomes is compromised when ATG9A is absent (viral inclusions fail to mount near the ER) and less complete genomes are produced ( Fig 7F ). In fact, we showed that there is a significant accumulation of all vRNP types in the cell cytosol upon ATG9A depletion ( Fig 7A and 7B ). This is consistent with a blockade in viral genome assembly distinct from viral transmembrane protein production and transport and points toward a defect in the efficiency of complete genomes formation in the cell. The accumulation of transmembrane proteins at the surface results from reduced budding and release of virions ( Fig 7C ). The concept that ATG9A is a modulator of liquid–liquid phase separation on or near ER in mammalian cells has also been recently proposed by another group [ 22 ]. ATG9A regulates phase separation and spatial organization of the autophagosome component FIP200 on the ER tubules. Interestingly, FIP200 condensates associate and move along the ER strand and enlarge via growth or fusion, with ATG9A dynamically orbiting FIP200 condensates in a manner similar to viral inclusions ( Fig 4D–4F ). Whether ATG9A acts directly to locally coordinate phase separation of viral inclusions or indirectly via its lipid scramblase activity to remodel the ER is yet to be determined. On one hand, ATG9A has 3 putative disordered regions ( www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q7Z3C6/entry ), thought to be important for biomolecular condensate formation [ 61 ], which could hint that it has a direct role in phase separation. One of these regions is actually very large in the N-terminus. On the other hand, being a scramblase, ATG9A may directly affect the membrane curvature tensions on both sides of the lipidic bilayer. So if some external entity tries to deform a membrane (in our case, it could be the vRNPs), a scramblase could help diminish the effort to induce curvature [ 62 ]. Understanding the mechanisms controlling the material properties of viral inclusions formed during IAV infection may provide new means to prevent IAV genome assembly. Future directions should involve identifying the interacting partners of ATG9A (as ATG2A has been excluded as such in our system) and the signaling pathways that promote phase separation of viral inclusions at the ER. The unveiled key biological processes may have extended relevance to other severe viral infections, which involve ER remodeling and phase separation, for example, hepatitis C virus and SARS-CoV-2. Methods Cells and viruses The epithelial cells Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) and alveolar basal (A549) were a kind gift of Prof Paul Digard, Roslin Institute, United Kingdom. The GFP-Rab11a WT low and DN low stable cell lines (in A549 background) were previously produced and characterized by us [ 4 , 6 ]. All cell types were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, Gibco, 21969035) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, 10500064), 1% penicillin/streptomycin solution (Biowest, L0022) and 2 mM L-glutamine (Gibco). GFP-Rab11 WTlow and DNlow cell culture media was also supplemented with 1.25 μg.mL −1 puromycin (Calbiochem). Cells were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination with the LookOut mycoplasma PCR detection kit (Sigma, MP0035), using JumpStart Taq DNA Polymerase (Sigma, D9307). Reverse genetics derived A/Puerto Rico/8/34 (PR8 WT; H1N1) virus and PR8 virus expressing PA-mNeonGreen [ 16 ] were used as model viruses and titrated by plaque assay according to reference [ 6 ]. Virus infections were performed at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 3 to 10. After 45 min, cells were overlaid with DMEM containing either 0.14% bovine serum albumin (for plaque assays) or DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin/streptomycin solution, and 2 mM L-glutamine (for immunofluorescence, western blotting, and RT-qPCR). To calculate viral titers, supernatants collected from infected cells were subjected to a plaque assay on MDCK monolayers. The drug nocodazole (Sigma, 487928) was dissolved in DMSO and used at a final concentration of 10 μg.mL −1 for 2 h. Plasmids and siRNA Reverse genetic plasmids were contributed by Dr Ron Fouchier (Erasmus MC, the Netherlands). The GFP-tagged ATG9A plasmid was a gift from Dr Sharon Tooze (Francis Crick Institute, UK). The plasmid encoding mCherry tagged to the ER was produced in-house and characterized by us in [ 4 ]. The siRNA targeting ATG9A (mixture of 4 siRNAs, GS79065), ATG2A (mixture of 4 siRNAs, GS23130), ULK1 (1 siRNA type, SI02223270), ULK2 (mixture of 4 siRNAs, GS9706), TBC1D14 (mixture of 4 siRNAs, GS57533), and non-targeting (NT, #5091027310) were purchased from Qiagen. Transfections For plasmid transfection, cells were grown to 70% confluency in 24-well plates and transfected with 250 ng of indicated plasmids using Lipofectamine LTX and Opti-MEM (both from Life Technologies), according to manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were simultaneously transfected and infected or mock-infected with PR8 virus, at MOI 10, for 8 to 12 h. Specifically for GFP-ATG9A overexpression, plasmid transfection was performed 24 h before infection. For siRNA transfection, cells were grown to 50% confluency in 6-well plates the day before transfection. Cells were transfected with siRNA (100 pmol/well) using DharmaFECT (Dharmacon) for 48 h and then infected or mock-infected with PR8 at MOI 3 for 8 h. High-pressure freezing/freeze substitution and electron tomography Cells grown on 3 mm aclar disks (carbon coated) were fixed using a mixture of 2% (v/v) formaldehyde and 0.2% (v/v) glutaraldehyde (Polysciences) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer, for 2 h at RT. Cells in the aclar disks were added to a 0.04-mm deep carrier filled with 1-hexadecene and frozen using a High Pressure Freezer Compact 02 (Wohlwend Engineering Switzerland). The samples were then freeze substituted at −90°C with 0.1% (w/v) uranyl acetate and 0.01% (w/v) tannic acid (EMS) in acetone for 6 h using a Leica EM AFS2 with a processor Leica EM FSP. The temperature was then raised to −45°C at a slope of 5°C/h. Samples were stabilized at −45°C for 1.5 h before washing in acetone 3 times. Samples were infiltrated and embedded in Lowicryl HM20 (Polysciences) at −45°C. Polymerization of the resin was done using UV light at −25°C for 48 h. Sections of 120 nm (Leica UC7) were picked on palladium-copper grids coated with 1% (w/v) formvar (Agar Scientific) in chloroform (VWR). The post-staining was made with 1% (w/v) uranyl acetate and Reynolds lead citrate, for 5 min each. For tomography, 15 nm protein A-gold (UMC, Utrecht) was added to both sides of the sections before staining, as fiducial markers. Tilt-series were acquired on a FEI Tecnai G2 Spirit BioTWIN operating at 120 keV equipped with an Olympus-SIS Veleta CCD Camera. The images were aligned based on the fiducial markers, and tomograms were reconstructed and joined with the IMOD toolbox [ 63 ]. Manual segmentation of cell organelles was used to generate 3D surface models using the AMIRA software (Thermo Scientific). Tokuyasu—Double immunogold labeling Cells were fixed in suspension using 2% (v/v) formaldehyde (EMS) and 0.2% (v/v) glutaraldehyde (Polysciences) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PB), for 2 h at RT. Subsequently, cells were centrifuged and washed with PB. The aldehydes were quenched using 0.15% (w/v) glycine (VWR) in 0.1 M PB for 10 min at RT. Cells were infiltrated in 12% (w/v) gelatin (Royal) for 30 min at 37°C and centrifuged. The gelatin was solidified on ice, cut into 1 mm 3 cubes, and placed in 2.3 M sucrose (Alfa Aesar) in 0.1 M PB, overnight at 4°C. The cubes were mounted onto specimen holders and frozen at −196°C by immersion into liquid nitrogen. Samples were trimmed and cut into 50-nm-thick sections (in a Leica EM-FC7 at −110°C) and laid onto formvar carbon-coated 100-mesh grids. For immunogold labeling, sections were blocked with PBS/1% BSA for 20 min at RT. Antibody staining was done sequentially in PBS/1% BSA at RT: rabbit anti-GFP (1:500, 1 h, Abcam, 6556), goat anti-rabbit IgG conjugated to 18 nm gold (1:20, 30 min; Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories, 111-215-144), mouse anti-NP (1:200, 1 h, Abcam, 20343), and goat anti-mouse IgG conjugated with 6 nm gold (1:20, 30 min; Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories, 115-195-146). Gold particles were fixed by applying 1% (v/v) formaldehyde in PBS for 5 min at RT. Blocking and extensive washing were performed in-between stainings. In the final step, gold particles were fixed using 1% (v/v) glutaraldehyde (Polysciences) for 5 min at RT. Grids were washed in distilled H 2 O and counterstained using methyl-cellulose–uranyl acetate solution for 5 min on ice. EM images were acquired on a Hitachi H-7650 operating at 100 keV equipped with a XR41M mid-mount AMT digital camera. Images were postprocessed using Adobe Photoshop CS2 and ImageJ (NIH). Fixed-cell imaging For immunofluorescence, cells were fixed for 15 min with 4% formaldehyde and permeabilized for 7 min with 0.2% (v/v) Triton-X-100 in PBS. Cells were incubated with the indicated primary antibodies for 1 h at RT, washed and incubated for 30 min with Alexa Fluor–conjugated secondary antibodies and Hoechst. Antibodies used were as follows: rabbit polyclonal against Rab11a (1:200; Proteintech, 15903-1-AP), ATG9A (1:200, Abcam, 108338), and viral NP (1:1,000; gift from Prof Paul Digard, Roslin Institute, UK); mouse monoclonal against viral NP (1:1,000; Abcam, 20343), PDI (1:500, Life Technologies, MA3-019), GM130 (1:500, BD Transduction Laboratories, 610823); mouse monoclonal against alpha-tubulin (1:1,000; b5-1-2, Sigma, T6074). Actin was stained using 100 nM of phalloidin-iFluor488 for 30 min at RT (Phalloidin-iFluor 488 Reagent, ab176753). Secondary antibodies were all from the Alexa Fluor range (1:1,000; Life Technologies). Following washing, cells were mounted with Dako Faramount Aqueous Mounting Medium, and single optical sections were acquired on either a Leica SP5 live confocal or a Zeiss LSM 980 AiryScan2 system. Live-cell imaging Cells (2 × 10 4 /well) were grown in chambered glass-bottomed dishes (Lab-Tek) and maintained at 37°C, 5% CO 2 in Opti-MEM medium (Gibco) during imaging. Samples were imaged using either a Roper Spinning Disk confocal (Yokogawa CSU-X1) or a Zeiss LSM 980 AiryScan2 systems and postprocessed using Adobe Photoshop CS2 and ImageJ (NIH). For microtubule staining in live cells, 200 nM of Sir-Tubulin (Cytoskeleton) was added 10 h before imaging. Quantitative image analysis Circularity and roundness: For shape quantifications of viral inclusions in confocal optical sections of fixed samples, we first segmented the periphery (using Rab11a or NP staining) of the cell and the nucleus (Hoechst staining), then the nucleus was removed, followed by segmentation of the cytoplasmic viral inclusions (using Rab11a or NP staining) using a custom-made macro and ImageJ [ 64 ]. Briefly, the background of images was subtracted, thresholds adjusted automatically, and “shape descriptor” function used to determine the roundness/circularity of each viral inclusion inside selected cells. Frequency distributions were calculated and plotted with GraphPad Prism using intervals of circularity/roundness values between [0–1]. Images were postprocessed using Adobe Photoshop CS2 and ImageJ. Mean squared displacement: Trackmate plugin [ 65 ] was used to track the XY trajectories of viral inclusions for 10 min at a timescale of 2 s/frame in live cells, and their MSD was subsequently analyzed with a custom R (version 4.1.0) script, using the formula MSD = (x(t) − x(0)) 2 + (y(t) − y(0)) 2 . Manders’ colocalization: Before colocalization analysis, we performed noise reduction of spinning disk confocal images of live-cell imaging using an implementation of noise2void [ 66 ] in ZeroCostDL4mic [ 67 ]. Since intensities are not guaranteed to be linear after this enhancement, and we were mainly interested in testing overlap (or co-occurrence) and not correlation of fluorescence intensities between microtubules (tubulin) and viral inclusions (Rab11a or PA-mNeonGreen), we opted for Manders’ co-occurrence analysis. We calculated the thresholded Manders’ Overlap Coefficient (tM1) for microtubules as a measurement of association of viral inclusions with microtubules, which ensures that tM1 is irrespective of the size or shape of the viral inclusions, which would result in a biased estimation of co-occurrence. This was done at every 5 frames for each movie (10 min at a timescale of 2 s/frame). Colocalization analysis was performed in ImageJ using the “coloc2” plugin, and threshold values calculated automatically using Costes method [ 68 ] to avoid user bias. Pearson’s colocalization: Colocalization analysis in single sections of fixed cells to establish correlation of fluorescence intensities between structures (Rab11a versus NP; ATG9A versus GM130) was performed in ImageJ using the “colocalization threshold” plugin. Western blotting Western blotting was performed according to standard procedures and imaged using a LI-COR Biosciences Odyssey near-infrared platform or the Amersham chemiluminescence system. Antibodies used included the following: rabbit polyclonal against virus NP (1:1,000; a kind gift by Prof. Paul Digard, Roslin Institute, UK); rabbit polyclonal against ATG9A (1:500, Abcam, 108338); rabbit polyclonal against ATG2A (1:500, Proteintech, 23226-1-AP); mouse polyclonal against actin (1:1,000, Sigma, A5441); rabbit polyclonal against lamin B (1:1,000, Abcam, 16048); rabbit polyclonal against LC3 (1:1,000, MBL, PM0369). The secondary antibodies used were either from the IRDye range (1:10,000; LI-COR Biosciences) or linked to HRP (1:5,000; Cell Signaling Technologies, 1677074S). The original uncropped blots are included in S1 Raw Images. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting Cell monolayers (6 × 10 6 ) were trypsinized for 7 min at 37°C, centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 5 min, and cell pellets were resuspended in PBS containing 2% FBS. Approximately 1 × 10 6 cells/well were incubated for 30 min on ice with either PBS or with a monoclonal mouse antibody against viral proteins HA (neat, clone 6F6, produced in-house), NA (neat, clone 7D8, produced in-house), and M2 (1:400, clone 14C2, Abcam, 5416). Cells were then washed with PBS/2% FBS and centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 5 min for 3 consecutive rounds. Cells were then either incubated with PBS or with a secondary antibody against mouse IgG conjugated to Alexa 568 (1:1,000, Life Technologies). Several steps of washing and centrifugation were performed to remove the unbound antibody. Upon washing with PBS/2% FBS, cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde (2% PFA) at RT for 15 min, washed again in PBS, and analyzed in a BD Fortessa X-20 flow cytometer equipped with 4 lasers 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm, and 640 nm; an SSC detector; and 16 detectors 6V, 2A, 5A-V, and 3V. Transferrin recycling assay Cells (5 × 10 5 ) were serum starved in FBS-free DMEM for 2 h and then were incubated with 1 μg.mL −1 of Tf conjugated to Alexa Fluor 647 (Tf-647, Life Technologies, T-23366) for 10 min at 37°C, 5% CO 2 . Cells used to determine the level of Tf-647 internalization were quickly washed in PBS and detached with 1 mM EDTA before fixing in 2% PFA for 10 min. Cells used to quantify Tf-647 recycling were washed in PBS and then incubated for 5, 10, or 15 min in live cell imaging solution (LCIS, in-lab adaption of Thermo Fisher Scientific LCIS), washed in PBS, detached in 1 mM EDTA, and fixed in 2% PFA for 10 min. Fixed cells were then washed in PBS and filtered before analysis using the flow cytometer LSR Fortessa X20 (BD). Median fluorescence intensities of Tf-647 were measured and analyzed using the softwares FlowJo, GraphPad Prism, and a custom-made R script. Quantitative real-time reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) Extraction of RNA from samples in NZYol (NZYtech, MB18501) was achieved by using the Direct-zol RNA minipreps (Zymo Research, R2052). Reverse transcription (RT) was performed using the NZY first strand cDNA synthesis kit (NZYTech, MB12502). Real-time RT-PCR was prepared in 384-well, white, thin walled plates 384-well PCR Plate (ABgene 12164142) by using SYBR Green Supermix (Biorad, 172–5124), 10% (v/v) of cDNA and 0.4 μM of each primer. The reaction was performed on a ABI QuantStudio-384 machine (Applied Biosciences), under the following PCR conditions: Cycle 1 (1 repeat): 95°C for 2 min; Cycle 2 (40 repeats): 95°C for 5 s and 60°C for 30 s; Cycle 3: 95°C for 5 s and melt curve 65°C to 95°C (increment 0.05°C each 5 s). Standard curves were prepared by serially diluting 1:5 a mock-infected sample from each experiment. Data were analyzed using the QuantStudio 7 software (Applied Biosciences). The mRNA level of host factors was quantified relative to reference GAPDH mRNA level. Expression was normalized to mock-infected cells treated with control siRNA. Primer sequences used for real-time RT-qPCR are listed in S1 Data File (oligonucleotide sheet). In vitro synthesis of vRNA standards The strategy used in this study was published by [ 69 ]. The primers used to create templates containing a T7 phage promoter (TAATACGACTCACTATAGGG) sequence are listed in S1 Data File (oligonucleotide sheet). Viral gene sequences in pPolI plasmids for all PR8 segments were amplified by PCR using corresponding primer pairs and were purified using ZYMO Research DNA cleaner and Concentrator-5 (ZYMO, D4014). Purified PCR products were in vitro transcribed using the T7 RiboMAX Express Large Scale RNA Production System (Promega, P1320). The transcripts were purified using the RNeasy Micro kit (QIAGEN, 74004). The concentration of purified RNA was determined by spectrophotometry. The molecular copies of synthetic RNA were calculated based on the total molecular weight of the segment. RNA extraction from virions Supernatants from virus-infected cells were centrifuged at 6,800 g for 3 min to clear cryoprecipitates. Virion RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen, 52906) according to manufacturer’s instructions. The concentration of purified RNA was determined by spectrophotometry. Hot start reverse transcription with a tagged primer cDNAs complementary to vRNA (standards and RNA isolated from virions or infected cells) were synthesized with tagged primers to add an 18- to 20-nucleotide tag at the 5′ end that was unrelated to influenza virus (vRNAtag, GGCCGTCATGGTGGCGAAT). RT with the tagged primer was performed with the hot start method modification of using saturated trehalose, as described in [ 69 ]. vRNA-to-PFU ratio quantification Absolute quantification of vRNA levels in isolated virions was done by real-time RT-qPCR as described above. Standard curves were generated by 100-fold serial dilutions of synthetic viral RNA. Data were analyzed using the QuantStudio software (Applied Biosciences). Primer sequences used for RT and for real-time RT-qPCR are listed in S1 Data File (oligonucleotide sheet). The ratio of vRNA levels to PFUs (vRNA-to-PFU) was calculated by dividing vRNA levels in isolated virions by the PFUs obtained from the same cell supernatants. vRNA-to-GAPDH relative expression Quantification of vRNA levels in the cell cytosol was done by real-time RT-qPCR, having performed RT using the hot start method described above. Standard curves were prepared by serially diluting 1:5 an infected sample from each experiment. Data were analyzed using the QuantStudio 7 software (Applied Biosciences). The vRNA level of viral segments was quantified relative to reference GAPDH mRNA level. Expression was normalized to infected cells treated with control siRNA (siNT). Primer sequences used for real-time RT-qPCR are listed in S1 Data File (oligonucleotide sheet). Data quantification and statistical analysis Data were analyzed in Prism 6 version (GraphPad Software), in R (version 4.1.0), QuantStudio 7 software (Applied Biosciences), Adobe Photoshop CS2 version, AMIRA software (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and FlowJo. Experimental replicates and tests applied to determine statistical significance between different conditions are described in each figure legend.

title: Surface-modification of γ-Al2O3 pellets with organic phosphonic acids-quaternary ammonium compounds for adsorptive nitrate removal from water
content:
Abstract
The increased discharge of nitrate into natural waters, particularly in agriculturally impacted areas, has become a major challenge in water treatment because elevated nitrate concentrations are harmful to both human health and environmental equilibria. Therefore, the objective of this study is to present a novel method for the efficient adsorptive removal of nitrate from water. Regenerable γ-Al2O3-based adsorbers were prepared by surface functionalization with phosphonate-based quaternary ammonium modifiers synthesized in a two-step reaction. At an initial nitrate concentration of 50 mg L‒1, nitrate uptake increased rapidly to about 3.3 mg g‒1 within 60 min and reached a plateau of about 3.45 mg g‒1 after 120 min. Langmuir capacities ranged from 9.7 to 13.2 mg g‒1, with the highest value obtained for C2TMABr-modified Al2O3. Competing anions reduced nitrate uptake, with sulfate showing a substantially stronger inhibitory effect than chloride. Regeneration with 16.13 mmol L‒1 NaCl restored about 95% of the initial adsorption performance after 30 min, and the C2TMABr-modified adsorber retained 93 ± 2% of its initial capacity over the last seven of ten adsorption–desorption cycles. These results show that phosphonate-functionalized γ-Al2O3 pellets provide moderate nitrate uptake combined with practical separability, modifier-dependent selectivity, and good regeneration stability.

Introduction
In recent decades, the emission of contaminants into natural aquatic systems has increased significantly due to human activity []. Continuous industrialization and growing agriculture, specifically the resulting wastewater, as well as domestic sewage are the main sources for groundwater pollutants like heavy metals [] as well as nutrients like phosphate and nitrate [,,]. Of these increasing contaminants, caused by increasing agricultural and industrial activity, nitrate is one of the most common ions []. It is mainly discharged in agricultural activities via fertilization using excess amounts of synthetic nitrogenous fertilizers [] or employing liquid manure stemming from mass animal production []. These elevated nitrate levels in groundwater are a major environmental issue as groundwater is a main source for drinking water processing in many countries [].

Nitrate in drinking water can pose a risk to human health due to the formation of carcinogenic N-nitrosamines after ingestion [], an increased risk of stomach cancer [] as well as the development of methemoglobinemia in infants, also known as “blue baby syndrome” []. Besides human health risks, nitrate as an essential nutrient also interferes with natural equilibria in the environment by contributing to biomass growth []. Thus, high nitrate levels in aquatic ecosystems lead to an increase in lake eutrophication [] and red tides []. To combat these nitrate related issues, organizations like the WHO, European Union or German Environment Agency (GEA) have set nitrate concentration limits of 50 mg L‒1 in drinking water [–]. Nitrate is most commonly removed from industrial, agricultural, and municipal wastewater as well as groundwater using biological denitrification in which nitrobacteria reduce the ion to gaseous nitrogen (N2) [,]. Though the process generates high yields at low processing costs [], the method also requires a carbon source for the reduction and generates biological sludge that needs to be disposed of []. Other methods employ metals for a chemical reduction of the ion via nitrite (NO2-) to ammonia (NH3) and, lastly, nitrogen (N2). For these, the use of powdered aluminum (Al) [] or iron (Fe) hydroxides [] have been established, but new reductants like, e.g., nanosized iron particles [] or Zn/Ag bimetallic particles [] are being researched to increase efficiency of the process.

Besides these nitrate reducing methods, displacement methods like reverse osmosis (RO) or adsorption techniques also represent interesting nitrate removal methods. Though RO is a widely used process in the treatment of water [], the method shows rather low selectivity and is, therefore, usually combined with other treatment methods []. Adsorption, however, is a widely studied versatile method for the removal of various organic and inorganic pollutants with adsorbents ranging from carbon-based and agricultural materials to polymers and metal oxides/hydroxides [,–]. Several studies have summarized both established and emerging strategies for nitrate removal from water, including biological denitrification, membrane-based processes, ion exchange and adsorption, as well as the use of surface-modified adsorbents for improved nitrate uptake [,–]. These reviews show that adsorption remains particularly attractive when simple operation, modular use, and regeneration are desired. At the same time, they also highlight persistent limitations of many nitrate adsorbents, including insufficient selectivity in the presence of competing anions, incomplete regeneration data, and the lack of clear structure–property relationships for surface-bound functional groups.

To improve not only adsorption behavior, but also functionalities for other applications, surface modification of metal-based substrates like zeolites [], TiO2 [], indium tin oxide (ITO) [,], Al2O3 (alumina) []. and others [,–] is investigated extensively. Aluminum oxides (Al₂O₃) are considered promising materials for nitrate removal due to their high surface area, chemical stability, and adjustable surface properties. Notably, surface functionalization approaches can markedly improve their adsorption efficiency by introducing specific binding sites or altering surface charge characteristics. Drastic improvements in adsorption behavior through surface functionalization via amine or ammonium containing surfactants or silane coupling agents are known for clay minerals [,], silicas [], zeolites [] and other inorganic materials [].

One interesting class of modifiers for metal oxides are phosphonic acids (PAs) and the corresponding esters due to their ability to form highly dense self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) [] that are stable against hydrolysis thanks to the formation of a strong P-O-metal bond []. In addition, these monolayers exhibit high mechanical stability as well as good stability in alkaline media [] which makes them suitable for application in, e.g., gas separation [] and organic photovoltaic devices []. Formation of the SAM occurs by a condensation reaction of the phosphonic acid with hydroxy groups present on the metal oxide surface []. This process is catalyzed by Lewis acid sites which facilitate the donor-acceptor interaction between PA and MO, making the P atom more electrophilic, thus, promoting the reaction [].

Against this background, the present study investigates a pellet-based γ-Al2O3 platform bearing phosphonate-anchored quaternary ammonium groups and examines how modifier structure influences nitrate uptake, selectivity, and regenerability. Nitrate was chosen as the primary target because this work focuses on ground- and drinking water treatment, where nitrate is a key regulated contaminant. In contrast, sulfate and chloride were included as representative competing ions to assess selectivity, while nitrite and phosphate were considered outside the main scope of the present study due to their different occurrence patterns and treatment contexts.

Results and discussion

Modifier synthesis

For the design of the required modifier structures, we regarded two key components: an anchoring group for the covalent attachment of the modifier to the metal oxide and a functionality for the adsorption of nitrate ions in aqueous media. These functionalities are connected by an alkyl chain, keeping the structures as simple as possible as well as maintaining water solubility of the modifiers. For the surface anchoring group of the modifier, we chose phosphonic acids which are highly suitable as surface modifiers due to the presence of three oxygen atoms, therefore primarily forming tridentate bonds on metal oxide surfaces []. Compounds containing phosphonic acids are also synthetically easily accessible via simple Michaelis-Arbuzov-reactions of triethyl phosphite with various alkyl or aryl halides and subsequent conversion of the phosphonic esters to acids []. This pathway also bears the advantage of the formation of a base-stable protecting group that can be cleaved at the appropriate step of the synthesis.

Adsorption sites of the modifiers were chosen to be quaternary ammonium salts which act as ion exchangers to exchange a halide ion for a nitrate ion from the water as this functionality is already researched and employed in polymeric nitrate ion exchange resins []. Both functionalities are connected by alkyl chains which are varied in length with an ethyl chain 6, a butyl chain 7–9 as well as a hexyl chain 10 (Fig 1).

The synthetic route for the surface-modifiers is shown in Fig 1. The syntheses for modifiers 6–10 commenced with the conversion of dibromo alkanes to (diethyl) phoshono bromides by using a reported Michaelis-Arbuzov reaction []. For these reactions, triethyl phosphite (TEP) was employed with the respective dibromo alkane 1–2 in a 1:4 ratio to prevent double substitution. The process required freshly distilled starting materials to achieve high yields of the desired products 4 and 5.

Bromo phosphonates 3–5, including the commercial diethyl (2-bromoethyl) phosphonate 3, were then converted to the quaternary ammonium salts 6–10 by treatment with an amine solution in either iso-propanol or EtOH in a Menshutkin reaction and subsequent deprotection of the phosphonic acid.

The first steps of the reactions were performed at room temperature in a closed vessel to avoid volatilization of the amine over the course of several days (Fig 1). Monitoring of the reaction with trimethyl amine (TMA) via 1H-NMR spectroscopy showed that compound 6 containing the shortest alkyl chain reacted more readily than the C4- and C6-chain compounds 7 and 10 taking seven days for full conversion as the influence of the phosphonate group on the substituted carbon decreases with an increasing chain length between the moieties. Quaternized intermediate compounds also exhibited rather strong hygroscopicity making isolation and purification of the substances difficult. Solvents and excess amine were removed via vacuum distillation resulting in a pale-yellow oil immiscible with most organic solvents. 1H-NMR analysis, however, confirmed the presence of water in the residue inhibiting crystallization of the compounds. Despite attempts towards optimization of the drying process, crystallization of the salts was not possible without high yield loss. We, therefore, decided to proceed with the synthesis without crystallization as it was unlikely that the residual water contamination interfered with the deprotection of the phosphonic acid. For the realization of modifiers 6, 7 and 10, the respective phosphono ammonium salts were deprotected under acidic conditions by refluxing the substances in conc. HCl. After removal of any excess acid and solvent, the crude products were dried thoroughly via repeated azeotropic distillation with iso-propanol which reduced the water content in the residue enough to make crystallization of the products possible.

To investigate the influence of the N-substituents on nitrate adsorption behavior, C4-modifiers containing a triethyl ammonium 8 and tripropyl ammonium group 9 were synthesized. Similar to the respective TMA modifier 12, phosphono bromide 4 was quaternized at room temperature using triethyl amine (TEA) in acetonitrile. Despite its higher basicity, reaction with TEA proceeded significantly slower than the respective reaction with TMA (see Table 1). Like other reported reactions of TEA [], the amine was used in 1.10 eq. with acetonitrile as a polar aprotic solvent to promote the desired substitution reaction. After a reaction time of 13 d, according to 1H-NMR analysis full conversion was achieved and after deprotection and work-up of the crude product a yield of 58% of isolated modifier 8 was obtained. Unlike reactions with TMA and TEA, quaternization with tripropyl amine (TPA) did not take place at room temperature. The reaction was, therefore, performed under reflux with an excess of 3.0 eq. of amine. The reaction proved successful after 3 d and yielded modifier 9 with 46% overall yield.

The overall yields shown in Table 1 represent the isolated compounds obtained from recrystallization in the last step of the synthesis. For characterization, compounds were fully purified to obtain crystals. For practical application on a larger scale in the future, however, this would not be necessary. Yield loss due to hygroscopic properties during the crystallization process could, therefore, be avoided by preparing stock solutions of the crude products to be used for surface modification of Al2O3. To maintain consistency in surface loading during the process of surface modification, concentrations of the modifier solutions could be determined by, e.g., NMR spectroscopy.

Characterization of surface-modified Al2O3

Upon contact with the phosphonic acid-based modifiers, the surface of Al2O3 is functionalized, whereby the positively charged ammonium group faces away from the surface and is available for adsorption processes. The Al-O-P bonds that form are very stable and often more durable than bonds created via silanols [,,], eliminating the hydrolysis issues typically associated with silane chemistry and thus enabling direct application in aqueous media. Evidence for successful functionalization was obtained by IR- and ³¹P-NMR-spectroscopy: in the IR spectrum (S1 Fig) at 2917 cm‒1 (vasCH2) and 2850 cm‒1 (vsCH2) the vibrations of the alkyl groups appear and in the range of 1060–1480 cm-1 there are bands attributed to P-O vibrational modes. In the ³¹P-NMR spectrum (S2 Fig), untreated alumina shows no signal, whereas functionalized samples such as C2TMABr exhibit a clear signal at 15.9 ppm, shifted to higher field compared to the free modifier (18.8 ppm), providing further confirmation of covalent attachment to the substrate. Complementary, elemental analysis shows that the overall modifier loadings are similar across all samples, with minor variations depending on the specific modifier. For modifiers containing TMABr or TEABr groups, the loadings are in a comparable range of 145 ± 4 µmol g‒1 (S1 Table). In contrast, the modifier bearing the TPABr group exhibits a slightly lower loading of about 130 µmol g‒1, which is likely attributable to the greater steric demand of the TPABr group. To further assess possible changes upon surface modification, N2 sorption measurements were performed for pristine and functionalized samples. The BET specific surface area remains in a very similar range after modification (219.8 m² g‒1 for pristine Al2O3 and 221.9–228.3 m² g‒1 for the modified samples). Likewise, the adsorption–desorption isotherms, pore size distributions, and cumulative pore volume curves show no significant differences. Overall, this data suggests that the mesoporous structure of the alumina support is largely preserved during functionalization and that no substantial pore blockage occurs (S3 Fig).

Nitrate adsorption investigations

Under the self-adjusted conditions of the adsorption system, the suspensions of the modified alumina pellets are in a narrow acidic range around pH 3.2, whereas unmodified Al2O3 shows a pH of 5.2 under otherwise identical conditions. The acidic pH of the modified adsorber suspensions is plausibly caused by residual acidic phosphonic acid functionalities. Since phosphonic acids can bind to metal oxide surfaces in mono-, bi-, or tridentate motifs, partially bound phosphonate groups may retain free P–OH groups that can deprotonate in water and contribute to the observed equilibrium pH. However, pH ~ 3.2 is not representative of typical drinking-water treatment conditions. Therefore, the adsorption data should be regarded as model experiments under self-adjusted acidic conditions. At near-neutral pH, the contribution of the protonated alumina surface is expected to decrease, whereas the permanently charged quaternary ammonium groups should retain ion-exchange capability.

At its native pH, unmodified Al2O3 adsorbs almost no nitrate over a period of 120 min. However, when the pH of the unmodified alumina suspension is adjusted to 3.2, a small but measurable nitrate uptake of about 0.4–0.5 mg g‒1 is observed after 120 min. This indicates that the positively charged alumina surface contributes to nitrate adsorption under acidic conditions. Nevertheless, the uptake remains far below that of the modified Al2O3 substrates, whose nitrate uptake increases rapidly to 3.3 mg g‒1 within 60 min and reaches a plateau of about 3.45 mg g‒1 after 120 min (Fig 2, S3 Fig). Thus, the enhanced adsorption of the modified pellets is governed mainly by the immobilized quaternary ammonium groups rather than by the native alumina surface alone under the conditions studied here.

More detailed information on the adsorption process can be derived from the data on time-dependent adsorption by applying kinetic models. While in adsorption according to the Pseudo-First-Order (PFO) model there are no or only minor chemical interactions between adsorbate and adsorbent and the adsorbent surface is considered homogeneous, the opposite is the case in adsorption according to the Pseudo-Second-Order (PSO) model. Here, stronger interactions between adsorbate and adsorbent are assumed, e.g., due to different electrical charges and heterogeneous surfaces. In the case of PFO, the adsorption rate is determined by the mass transport of the adsorbate to the surface and its accumulation at adsorption sites; in the case of PSO, it is also determined by the reaction kinetics at the active center. Fig 3 shows the linear plots (Equations 2 and 4; S1 File) for the nitrate adsorption on the different modified substrates for each kinetic model. For [수식] the [수식] values at 120 min were used. The resulting values for [수식] , [수식] , [수식] and R² obtained by applying Equation 2 and 4 as well as by curve fitting via equation 3 and 5 (S1 File) are listed in Table 2.

The data show that all tested substrates have a high linear agreement with the theoretical equations (R² > 0.99) in both kinetic models, with a slightly higher agreement for the PSO model, if plots via Equation 2 and 4 are compared.

Although the linearized PSO plots give slightly higher R² values, the non-linear PFO fits reproduce the experimental adsorption curves and especially the equilibrium adsorption capacities more accurately. This is also evident from the kinetic profiles for C2TMABr shown in Fig 4, where the PFO model reproduces the experimental adsorption behavior more closely than the PSO model. The PSO model systematically overestimates [수식] , whereas the PFO model yields values close to the experimental ones. This can be rationalized by the experimental conditions used for the kinetic measurements. In these experiments, 0.5 g of adsorbent is contacted with 50 mL of a 50 mg L-1 nitrate solution, corresponding to a total nitrate amount of only 2.5 mg and thus to a maximum possible loading of 5.0 mg g-1. This value is well below the adsorption capacities obtained from the isotherm analysis, indicating that the kinetic experiments are carried out under underloaded conditions. In addition, nitrate uptake is rather rapid during the initial stage and approaches a plateau after about 60 min. Under these conditions, the PFO model appears to provide the more appropriate empirical description of nitrate uptake, whereas the PSO model tends to overestimate the equilibrium loading. Similar observations have also been discussed in literature with Revellame et al. [] pointing out that the PFO model can be equally valid, or in some cases even more suitable, than the PSO model for describing adsorption processes.

Adsorption isotherms and adsorption capacity

To test adsorption capacity of the modified substrates and obtain further information on the adsorption mechanism, the nitrate uptake in solutions with different nitrate concentrations is investigated after equilibration. The Langmuir model assumes a finite number of free, energetically equivalent adsorption sites, each of which can only be occupied by one molecule (formation of a monolayer). Furthermore, there are no interactions between adsorbed molecules. In the Langmuir model, adsorption increases with increasing concentration but saturates and thus leads to maximum loading. In the case of Freundlich, there is a heterogeneous surface with energetically different adsorption sites, and adsorption energy of adsorbents decreases exponentially the more saturated the surface becomes. Fig 5 shows the linearized form of the Langmuir and Freundlich equations (S2 File) as an example for C2TMABr.

From these linearized forms, [수식] or n can be obtained as the slopes of the straight lines and [수식] or [수식] from the points of intersection with the y-axis. The corresponding values for the different adsorbers are listed in Table 3.

As can be seen from the data, both models describe the behavior of the adsorber well and high values for R² are obtained in both cases, although the Freundlich model seems to fit better overall. This is plausible since an increasing loading of the adsorber with negatively charged nitrate ions leads to an increasingly electrically balanced surface, whereby the interactions with new adsorbates steadily decrease. The values obtained by applying the Freundlich model for n above 1 also indicate a moderately pronounced surface heterogeneity. The values obtained for [수식] hardly differ between the adsorbents used except for C6TMABr where [수식] is slightly increased. Higher [수식] values indicate a stronger interaction between adsorbate and adsorbent. Similarly, [수식] is also increased in the Langmuir model for C6TMABr, indicating a stronger affinity between nitrate and adsorbent surface.

The adsorber capacities [수식] determined via Langmuir decrease with increasing chain length of the modifier for both the aliphatic linker and the N-substituents. The value of 13.2 mg g-1 determined for C2TMABr agrees with the experimentally found value. To obtain this value, the adsorber modified with C2TMABr is used several times in nitrate solutions with a nitrate content of 50 mg L-1 without desorbing it in between. Fig 6 shows the amount of nitrate adsorbed in each adsorption cycle and the cumulative amount of nitrate adsorbed over the number of adsorption cycles. After the eighth adsorption, an increasing saturation of the adsorber becomes apparent with a cumulative amount of nitrate is 11.4 mg g-1. It should be noted that the present materials are designed as pellet-based, readily separable adsorbents rather than as dispersed high-surface-area powder systems. Therefore, absolute capacity comparisons with nanoparticulate or finely powdered adsorbents are only of limited practical relevance. A more meaningful assessment is obtained by relating nitrate uptake to the loading of immobilized surface functionalities. Elemental analysis shows modifier loadings of 145 ± 4 µmol g‒1 for the TMABr- and TEABr-containing materials and 130 µmol g‒1 for the TPABr-containing material, while the maximum nitrate adsorption capacities range from 9.7 to 13.2 mg g‒1. Thus, nitrate uptake is in the same order of magnitude as the density of immobilized quaternary ammonium sites, and the capacity trend across the series follows the modifier loading closely. This strongly suggests that nitrate adsorption is primarily governed by the covalently immobilized quaternary ammonium groups and that these sites are utilized with high efficiency.

Compared to previously reported inorganic nitrate adsorbents, the present phosphonate-functionalized γ-Al2O3 materials show a moderate adsorption capacity in absolute terms. The best-performing adsorber, C2TMABr-modified Al2O3, reached a Langmuir capacity of 13.2 mg g⁻¹. However, direct comparison with literature systems is only indicative, because adsorbent form, specific surface area, and experimental conditions differ substantially. For example, ammonium-functionalized mesoporous silicas were investigated as fine powdered adsorbents and still exhibited very high BET surface areas of 351–890 m² g⁻¹ after functionalization, together with nitrate adsorption capacities of about 25–46.5 mg g⁻¹. In contrast, cetylpyridinium bromide-modified zeolite was used as a powder fraction below 75 µm and reached a maximum nitrate capacity of 9.36 mg g⁻¹, while no BET surface area was reported for that system. Accordingly, the present materials are best understood not as record-capacity adsorbents, but as a pellet-based ceramic platform with covalently phosphonate-anchored ion-exchange sites, preserved textural properties, and good regeneration stability.

A comparison with polymer-based nitrate-selective ion-exchange resins is also relevant, since these materials represent the most established adsorption-type technology for nitrate removal. In absolute terms, commercial nitrate-selective resins generally offer higher exchange capacities and often better practical selectivity than the present ceramic adsorbers []. However, these compounds represent a fundamentally different material class. In the present work, the objective was not to reproduce the performance of conventional polymer resins, but to establish a regenerable ceramic platform in which quaternary ammonium ion-exchange sites are covalently immobilized via phosphonate anchoring on a pelletized inorganic support. In this context, the observed modifier-dependent selectivity trend is particularly noteworthy, as it is consistent with previous reports on nitrate-selective trialkyl amine-based resins, where increasing hydrophobicity of the functional groups improved nitrate preference [].

Effect of interfering ions

In real water applications, nitrate is typically not present in isolation, but in combination with a large number of other dissolved ions. An adsorber that is to be used specifically to remove nitrate should therefore interact as little as possible with foreign ions in the solution to be treated, so as to avoid competition for free adsorption sites. For this reason, it was tested how the nitrate uptake of the differently modified adsorbers is influenced by the presence of frequently accompanying anions, chloride and sulfate. Fig 7 shows that all functionalized adsorbers achieve the highest loadings of nitrate in pure nitrate solutions and differ only marginally in terms of loading. The presence of foreign ions such as chloride or sulfate results in reduced nitrate uptake for all tested adsorbers. Nitrate uptake is inhibited with an increasing concentration of foreign ions, in which sulfate ions have a significantly more negative effect on nitrate adsorption than chloride ions. This circumstance is a well-known problem in the field of nitrate adsorption [].

The stronger adsorption of sulfate and chloride compared to nitrate can be explained by two main factors. First, ion exchange selectivity is largely determined by the hydration energy of the competing anions. Ions with lower hydration energy are more easily dehydrated and therefore interact more easily with the functional groups of the resin. Nitrate (ΔG° = −314 kJ mol‒1) has a lower hydration energy than chloride (−363 kJ mol‒1) and especially sulfate (−1103 kJ mol‒1), so nitrate is generally preferred. However, the relatively high hydration energies of chloride and especially sulfate mean that these ions can still effectively compete for exchange sites under certain conditions, especially when present in higher concentrations. Secondly, the nature of the functional groups on the resin has a strong influence on selectivity. Longer alkyl chains, such as the triethyl- or tripropyl ammonium groups, increase hydrophobicity of the adsorber material, which in turn reduces the hydration of anions at the interface between resin and solution. This effect favors the uptake of ions with lower hydration energies, such as nitrate, over more hydrated species like sulfate [].

This is reflected in the behavior of the various modified adsorbers. While adsorbers with TMABr as the functional group behave almost identically in nitrate adsorption in the presence of foreign ions, the selectivity for nitrate increases in adsorbers with increasing hydrophobicity of the N-substituents from TEABr to TPABr, especially in the presence of sulfate. In contrast, the length of the spacer chain has little to no impact, as its position between the functional group and the aluminum oxide surface makes it largely inaccessible to competing anions; consequently, its potential hydrophobic effect is not as pronounced as expected.

At the same time, the data clearly shows that sulfate tolerance of the present materials is still limited in absolute terms. Although increasing hydrophobicity of the quaternary ammonium substituents improves nitrate preference under competitive conditions, sulfate causes a pronounced decrease in nitrate uptake for all investigated adsorbers. Therefore, the current materials should not be regarded as highly sulfate-resistant nitrate adsorbers. Rather, the results demonstrate a structure–selectivity relationship within this phosphonate-functionalized ceramic adsorber platform and indicate that further optimization will be necessary for applications in sulfate-rich waters. In practical terms, the present materials appear most suitable for nitrate-contaminated waters with low to moderate sulfate contents or as regenerable, readily separable proof-of-concept adsorbers for water treatment.

Desorption tests

Another important feature of adsorbers is their ability to be regenerated, which enables repeated applications and thus offers both ecological and economic advantages. Rinsing loaded adsorbers with concentrated NaCl solutions is a widely used approach, in which a large proportion of adsorbed nitrate is displaced from the adsorption sites due to the large excess of chloride present. Experiments were carried out to test which NaCl concentrations and desorption times are necessary to effectively remove bound nitrate from the adsorber. For this purpose, C2TMABr pellets loaded with nitrate were desorbed, then subjected to nitrate adsorption again and the adsorption capacity compared with non-desorbed pellets (Fig 8). As seen in Fig 8A, the adsorber without prior desorption only adsorbs around 73% of the amount of nitrate during the second adsorption cycle compared to a fresh, unused adsorber.

As vacant sites are already filled with nitrate during the first adsorption cycle, the driving force for adsorbing further nitrate ions in the second adsorption cycle decreases noticeably. If the adsorber is rinsed with a solution of 4.03 mmol L-1 NaCl for 2 h after the first adsorption, around 90% of the original nitrate load is achieved in the subsequent adsorption cycle. This value can be increased to around 96% with increasing chloride concentration to 16.13 mmol L-1. The faster the desorption takes place, the shorter the downtime of the adsorber in potential applications. As the solution with 16.13 mmol L-1 NaCl provided the best desorption results in the previous test, it is necessary to investigate the extent to which the desorption time of 2 h could be further reduced. Fig 8B shows the relative nitrate uptake after different desorption times. A clear increase in adsorption performance compared to the non-desorbed adsorber can be seen after just 5 min. For an adsorption performance of 95% of the initial value, 30 min proves to be sufficient.

In addition to desorption capacity, regeneration stability is also an important metric. The adsorber material should withstand as many adsorption and desorption cycles as possible without any noticeable loss of adsorption capacity. To test regeneration stability of the C2TMABr modified adsorber, a total of 10 adsorption/desorption cycles were carried out (Fig 8C). Adsorption was carried out for 120 min in a solution with 50 mg L-1 nitrate followed by desorption with 16.13 mmol L-1 NaCl solution for 30 min. It is shown that the modified adsorber reliably adsorbs nitrate even after higher numbers of desorption/adsorption cycles, despite larger fluctuations in individual measured values. On average, nitrate uptake of around 93% (± 2%) was achieved over the last seven adsorption cycles compared to the initial value, which indicates that the C2TMABr surface modification remains stable over repeated adsorption–desorption cycles and is not washed out to a significant extent under the applied regeneration conditions.

Compared to previously established nitrate-removal methods, the present phosphonate-functionalized γ-Al2O3 pellets should not be regarded as a replacement for high-throughput technologies such as biological denitrification or membrane-based separation, nor do they match the absolute exchange capacity of commercial nitrate-selective resins. Instead, their relevance lies in a different performance profile: the active quaternary ammonium sites are covalently immobilized on a pelletized ceramic support, the textural properties of the support are largely preserved, and effective regeneration with NaCl is possible over repeated cycles. Thus, the present system offers moderate nitrate uptake in absolute terms, but combines practical separability, structural tunability, and regeneration stability in a way that may be attractive for modular or regenerable adsorption-based treatment concepts. At the same time, the strong competition by sulfate shows that further optimization is required before broader application in complex water matrices can be envisaged.

Conclusion
This study demonstrates that γ-Al2O3 pellets functionalized with phosphonate-bound quaternary ammonium groups represent a regenerable and structurally tunable ceramic adsorber platform for nitrate removal from aqueous solutions. Surface modification markedly enhanced nitrate uptake compared to unmodified alumina, and under the present experimental conditions the adsorption kinetics were described more appropriately by the Pseudo-First-Order (PFO) model. Adsorption isotherm analysis showed that both Langmuir and Freundlich models provided good fits, with Freundlich giving a slightly better description, indicating a moderately heterogeneous surface and decreasing interaction energy at higher loadings. The presence of competing anions reduced nitrate adsorption, with sulfate exerting a substantially stronger inhibitory effect than chloride. Variations in hydrophobicity of the quaternary ammonium substituents influenced selectivity, especially in sulfate-containing systems, whereas the length of the spacer chain between the functional group and the alumina surface had negligible impact. Desorption tests showed that adsorbed nitrate could be effectively removed using NaCl solutions, and the C2TMABr-modified adsorbent retained over 90% of its initial capacity after multiple adsorption–desorption cycles, indicating good stability under the applied regeneration conditions. Although the maximum adsorption capacity is moderate in absolute terms compared with high-surface-area powdered adsorbents and commercial nitrate-selective ion-exchange resins, the present materials combine practical separability, covalently immobilized ion-exchange sites, preserved textural properties, and good regeneration stability.

The main contribution of this work is therefore not a record adsorption capacity, but the demonstration that phosphonate-based surface functionalization of γ-Al2O3 pellets provides a regenerable and structurally tunable nitrate adsorber platform with clear structure–property relationships. However, the strong competition by sulfate shows that further optimization of the surface functionality is required before practical application in sulfate-rich or otherwise complex water matrices can be envisaged. Future adsorber designs should therefore focus on improving nitrate selectivity under realistic multi-ion conditions, especially in the presence of sulfate.

Materials and methods

Reagents and analytical methods

Chemicals.
All chemicals in this work were purchased from either TCI or Sigma Aldrich and used without further purification unless stated otherwise. For azeotropic distillation and recrystallization, solvents were distilled and dried over 3 Å molecular sieves prior to use.

Spectroscopic methods.
1H-, 13C- and 31P-NMR analysis was performed on a Bruker Avance NEO 500 (500.18 MHz, 1H; 125.7 MHz, 13C; 202 MHz, 31P) and Bruker Avance I (300.13 MHz, 1H) with a 5 mm BBF-1H/D z-Grad probe head using CDCl3 and D2O as solvents at a temperature of 298 K. The signals were referenced by using the deuterated solvent signal. 31P solid-state NMR spectra of the functionalized particles were recorded on a 400 MHz Bruker Avance III HD NMR spectrometer using a 4 mm MAS sample head. Infrared spectroscopy was performed using a NicoletTM ISTM 5 FT-IR spectrometer with an iD7 ATR (diamond crystal) module. Thermo Scientific TM OMNICTM software was used to output the spectra. Measurements on functionalized particles were performed against background measurements on non-functionalized γ-Al2O3. The photometer used for nitrate analytics was a DR 6000 UV-VIS spectrophotometer from Hach.

Synthesis of surface modifiers

Detailed descriptions of the synthesis of surface modifiers can be found in the supporting information S1 Text.

Surface modification of Al2O3

The surface functionalization of the aluminum oxide substrates was carried out by adding 8 g of gamma aluminum oxide pellets to 50 mL of deionized water together with 4 mmol of the corresponding modifier and heated to 90 °C for 1 h. The pellets were then washed with deionized water to remove excess modifier from the surface and subsequently dried at 55 °C for 24 h.

Characterization of modified Al2O3

Textural properties of pristine and functionalized Al2O3 were analyzed by N2 sorptionAutosorb measurements using an iQ3 TPX by Quantachrom. The samples were dried at 120 °C overnight and measured with N2 at 77 K. The specific surface areas were calculated according to the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method. Pore size distributions and cumulative pore volumes were derived from the adsorption data.

The modifier content on the aluminum oxide pellets after functionalization was determined by measuring the carbon content via elemental analysis (Elementar vario MICRO cube). The amount of modifier in mmol per g total mass (Al2O3-pellet + modifier) can be calculated via Equation 1 with C% = percentage of carbon by mass and Mc = sum of the molar mass of C contained in the modifier compound (e.g., Mc for PnC2NBr = 5*12 = 60). Untreated pellets already have a C content of 0.35%, so all C values obtained for the functionalized pellets were adjusted by this value to determine the C content attributable to the modifiers. For qualitative investigations regarding surface bonding, IR- and 31P solid-state NMR spectra of the adsorbents were recorded (S1 Fig and S2 Fig).

 [수식] Equation 1

Nitrate analytics

The quantitative determination of nitrate in solution was carried out using a photometric method based on DIN standard 38405–9 []. In this method, nitrate in sulfuric acid solution is converted by 2,6-dimethylphenol to nitrophenol, which has an absorption maximum at a wavelength of 340 nm.

The solutions required for sample preparation were prepared in-house. A solution of 2,6-dimethylphenol in glacial acetic acid with a concentration of 1.2 g L-1 was prepared, stored at 4 °C, and renewed weekly. For the acid mixture, conc. H2SO4 and H3PO4 were mixed in a ratio of 1:1 (v/v) and stored at 4 °C. The solutions were warmed to RT before use.

For sample preparation, 250 µL of the nitrate solution to be determined was transferred to a reaction vessel. For samples with nitrate concentrations above 50 mg L-1, smaller sample volumes were taken and diluted with deionized water to obtain a total volume of 250 µL and a maximum nitrate content of 50 mg L-1. The samples were then mixed with 250 µL of the 2,6-dimethylphenol solution and 2 mL of the acid mixture. The reaction solution was stirred for 15 min at RT, then transferred to polystyrene cuvettes with a layer thickness of 1 cm and the absorbance measured at a wavelength of 340 nm. For each series of measurements, a blank sample with deionized water was prepared using the same procedure. The absorbance was measured three times and the mean value determined. To calculate the nitrate concentration based on the measured extinctions, a calibration curve was first created.

Performance of adsorption tests

For experiments to determine the adsorption kinetics, 0.5 g of the modified pellets were added to 50 mL of deionized water with a NO3- content of 50 mg L-1 (= 0.81 mmol L-1 NO3-; adjusted via KNO3) and stirred at RT. The pH of the adsorption suspensions was not externally adjusted in the standard adsorption experiments. Under these self-adjusted conditions, the suspensions containing modified alumina pellets were in a narrow acidic range around pH 3.2, whereas the suspension containing unmodified Al2O3 showed a pH of 5.2. To assess the contribution of the native alumina surface under acidic conditions, an additional control experiment was performed with unmodified Al2O3 after adjusting the suspension pH to 3.2.

Experiments to determine the adsorption isotherms were carried out equivalently with aqueous solutions of different NO3- contents in the range from 25 to 1000 mg L-1. Sampling was performed after 120 min. To experimentally determine the adsorption capacity of C2TMABr-modified pellets, 0.5 g of these were added eight times in succession to 50 mL of deionized water with a NO3- content of 50 mg L-1, stirred at room temperature, and then washed and dried. To determine the influence of anions on nitrate adsorption, 0.5 g of the modified pellets were placed in 50 mL of a NO3- solution in deionized water (50 mg L-1) with Cl- or SO42- (adjusted via NaCl or Na2SO4) in a molar ratio of anion/nitrate of 0.5:1, 1:1 and 2:1 and stirred for 120 min at RT. To test the regenerative capacity of the adsorbers, 0.5 g of C2TMABr-modified pellets were placed in 50 mL of a NO3- solution in water (50 mg L-1; adjusted via KNO3) for 120 minutes, stirred at RT, then washed and dried. The nitrate-loaded adsorbents were then added to 50 mL of deionized water containing 16.13, 8.06 or 4.03 mmol L-1 NaCl for different periods of time at RT. The pellets were then washed with deionized water, dried, and the nitrate uptake was tested again in an aqueous solution with a nitrate content of 50 mg L-1.

title: Vitamin D deficiency and clinical correlations in systemic sclerosis patients: A retrospective analysis for possible future developments
content: Introduction Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a connective tissue disease of multifactorial etiology, mainly characterized by microvascular damage followed by progressive fibrosis of skin and internal organs [ 1 ]. In SSc patients, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) serum concentrations have been shown and 25(OH)D deficiency was demonstrated to interfere with immune response [ 2 , 3 ]. Vitamin D seems to play a key role both on innate and adaptive immune system and the presence of its receptors on different cells types, seems to support this hypothesis. Especially in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis, a deficit in vitamin D serum concentrations is evident and seems to correlate with disease course and outcome [ 4 , 5 ]. Arnson et al. demonstrated, in a large multinational SSc patients’ population, that lower serum vitamin D concentrations were inversely correlated with the extent of cutaneous fibrosis. However, the effects of vitamin D supplements and seasonality of clinical assessments were not evaluated [ 6 ]. The purpose of the study was to correlate 25(OH)D serum concentrations, in a large cohort of SSc patients from two European referral centers, with clinical complications and seasonality. A further aim was to evaluate the efficacy of supplementation with oral colecalciferol in increasing 25(OH)D serum concentrations. Methods A population of 154 consecutive SSc patients (diagnosis based on LeRoy 2001 and later confirmed by 2013 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) criteria) was enrolled in the study [ 7 , 8 ]). 91 patients were followed up at the Rheumatology Division of Genoa University (Italy) and 63 at the Department of Rheumatology of Ghent University Hospital (Belgium). As part of the regular follow up approved by both Institutions for SSc, all patients undergone clinical evaluation and assessment of disease severity through the disease severity scale (DSS), developed by Medsger at al [ 9 ] ( Fig 1 ). Serum concentration of 25(OH)D was evaluated by the direct competitive chemi-luminescence DiaSorin LIAISON immunoassay (normal: 30–100 ng/ml). A concentration between 20 and 30 ng/ml was classified as 25(OH)D insufficiency, while concentrations <20 ng/ml referred as deficiency [ 10 ]. In all patients calcium concentrations were determined through COBAS, Roche Diagnostics Ltd, (normal: 8.5–10.5 mg/dl). In 44 patients also PTH serum concentrations was determined through DiaSorin LIAISON immunoassay (normal: 6.5–36 ng/l). 10.1371/journal.pone.0179062.g001 Fig 1 Medsger’s disease severity scale (DSS) parameters in the study population. In the left part of the figure, a graphic representation describes organ involvement through the distribution of the five values (0 to 4) for each parameter of Medsger’s DSS (white = none, light grey = mild, intermediate grey = moderate, dark grey = severe, black = end-stage). In the right part of the figure the same distribution is described in percentages (0 = none, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe, 4 = end-stage). Patients assuming oral cholecalciferol (Dibase Abiogen Pharma, Italy), at the recommended dose of 1,000 IU per day, for hypovitaminosis D prevention, were included in the study. On the same date, nailfold videocapillaroscopy (NVC) was performed in all patients by the same operator using an optical probe, equipped with a 200× contact lens, connected to an image analysis software (Videocap, DS Medica, Milan, Italy). Nailfold capillaries abnormalities were scored by a validated qualitative and semi-quantitative rating scale, in accordance with previous studies [ 1 , 11 – 13 ]. Pulmonary function test with diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO), chest x-ray, lung CT scan, electrocardiography (ECG), Doppler echocardiography with systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (sPAP) measurement, renal artery resistive index (RI) by echo color Doppler, were performed. Dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) was performed annually, according to National Osteoporosis Foundation guidelines, to calculate trabecular bone score (TBS) and bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine, hip, and proximal femur [ 14 ]. Drug assumption related effects were also evaluated ( S1 File ). All patients were informed that their data would be used for possible studies/analyses and gave their consent when starting to be followed up at the Clinic.
